pronunciation.note: Sūrya is Tier 1 because the initial ū is long. In Vedic usage, Sūrya is the visible disk of the sun, while Savitṛ is the sun as the power that impels sacrifice and life.

domains.title: The Eye of the World
domains.subtitle: Sun, Light, Health, and Cosmic Sight
domains.lead:
Sūrya is the sun not merely as a heavenly body but as the all-seeing eye of the cosmos. In the Ṛgveda he rises on his chariot, drawn by seven horses, and crosses the sky as the witness of every deed. He is the healer who drives away disease, the king who traverses the realms, and the hidden friend who sees what mortals do in secret.

His cult produced some of the most magnificent temples and rituals in South Asia, from the sandhya prayers performed at dawn and dusk to the great solar observatories of Jaipur and Delhi. Where other gods fade into myth, Sūrya remains tangible: every sunrise is his epiphany.

cards.name: Solar Chariot
cards.desc: He rides across heaven in a chariot drawn by seven horses, representing the days of the week or the colors of light.

cards.name: Healer and Eye
cards.desc: The sun removes darkness literally and metaphorically; his gaze is health, truth, and moral witness.

cards.name: Sandhyā Devotion
cards.desc: Twice-daily prayers at sunrise and sunset align the worshipper with the sun's renewing passage.

cards.name: Father of Time
cards.desc: The sun governs the year, the seasons, and the ritual calendar; his movement is the clock of dharma.

symbols.name: Seven horses

symbols.name: Lotus
symbols.meaning: The sun rising from the lotus, a symbol of emergence, purity, and renewal

symbols.name: Chariot and wheel (cakra)
symbols.meaning: The vehicle of the sun and the turning wheel of time and cosmic order

symbols.name: Ruby and gold
symbols.meaning: The colors and materials associated with solar radiance and kingship

symbols.meaning: In yoga, the inner sun is visualized within the heart lotus, the source of vital energy

mythology.lead: Sūrya's mythology is woven through the Vedas, epics, and Purāṇas. He is both a natural force and a divine person, the father of heroes and the relentless witness whose presence makes ethics possible.

myths.title: The Chariot of the Sun
myths.text: Ṛgveda 1.50 hymns Sūrya as the god who travels on a chariot yoked by the Aśvins, with swift horses and a golden seat. He is the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa, the spy of the whole world, the remover of darkness and the bringer of light. His rising is a daily renewal of cosmic law, and his rays are compared to arms stretched out over the earth.

myths.title: Sūrya's Descent as Sugrīva
myths.text: The monkey king Sugrīva, Rāma's ally in the war against Rāvaṇa, is born from Sūrya. This solar lineage gives him the speed, brightness, and royal dignity that make him indispensable to Rāma's campaign. It also reflects a broader pattern: Sūrya's children — Sugrīva, Yamarāja, the Aśvins, and Karṇa — are marked by energy, justice, or sacrifice.

myths.title: Karṇa, Son of the Sun
myths.text: Karṇa, the tragic hero of the Mahābhārata, is Sūrya's son by the unwed Kuntī. Born with golden armor and earrings that made him invincible, he was abandoned by his mother and raised by a charioteer. His loyalty to the Kauravas, his generosity, and his eventual death at Arjuna's hands make him one of the most moving figures in the epic, a son of the sun destroyed by the very radiance that marked him.

lore.syncretism: Sūrya was one of the few Vedic gods to retain and expand his worship into the medieval and modern periods, perhaps because the sun itself is impossible to demote. He absorbed Persian and Hellenistic solar imagery after the Indo-Greek and Kushan periods, and his iconography shows clear Greco-Roman influence in the boots, tunic, and royal attributes of classical Sūrya images. In Southeast Asia, the sun god appears in Cambodian and Javanese temple art, while in India the Saura tradition became one of the major religious streams. The Japanese Amaterasu, the Egyptian Rꜥ, and the Iranian Mithra are distant cousins in the broader ancient Near Eastern and Eurasian solar cult, though Sūrya's specific Vedic roots and his association with chariot, lotus, and healing mantras are distinctively Indic.
lore.culturalLegacy: Sūrya remains central to Hindu daily life. The Gāyatrī mantra, addressed to Savitṛ, is recited by millions at dawn; sūrya namaskāra, the sun salutation, is practiced in yoga classes worldwide. Sun temples such as Konark in Odisha and Modhera in Gujarat stand as architectural masterpieces of solar worship, while the Jantar Mantar observatories in Jaipur and Delhi translate his movement into monumental geometry. In Ayurveda and traditional medicine, sunlight is a healing force, and the sun's position determines auspicious moments (muhūrta) for every important undertaking. The name Sūrya is common across South Asia, and the sun continues to symbolize clarity, justice, and vital energy in popular culture.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Sūrya teaches that witnessing is a form of love. The sun does not judge; it simply sees, and in seeing, it makes life possible. Every secret act is held in its light, every shadow defined by its presence.

To worship Sūrya is to consent to be seen — not with shame but with the recognition that visibility is the condition of growth. The sun asks nothing in return but disciplined attention: the sandhya prayers at dawn and dusk, the alignment of breath with its rising and setting. In that attention, the cosmos becomes a ritual and the day itself a sacrament.

lore.archaeology: Images of Sūrya are among the most widespread in Indian art, from Kushan-period statuary showing Greco-Roman influence to the colossal chariot temple at Konark (13th century CE). The sun temple at Modhera (Gujarat) and the Martand temple in Kashmir preserve elaborate sculptural programs of solar mythology. Copperplate inscriptions and land grants frequently invoke Sūrya, and his cult was particularly strong in Odisha, Gujarat, Rajasthan, and Kashmir. The Jantar Mantar observatories in Jaipur and Delhi, built by Jai Singh II in the 18th century, are late but spectacular expressions of the royal interest in solar measurement.
